subject: Anthropology
title: Everyday Resistance
description: A micro-lesson that makes Everyday Resistance usable.

hook.text: Slaves broke tools. Peasants worked slowly. Workers called in sick. Resistance doesn't always look like revolution.

buildup.text: James Scott described weapons of the weak: foot-dragging, sabotage, gossip, and other quiet forms of resistance.

discovery.text: These hidden acts avoid direct confrontation but undermine the powerful. They're safer than open rebellion.

twist.text: Everyday resistance is often invisible to historians. It doesn't make headlines, but it constantly erodes domination.

climax.text: Power is never total. Even the most oppressed find ways to resist. Everyday acts of defiance shape history quietly.

punchline.text: The weak resist in whispers, not shouts.

quiz.question: What are weapons of the weak?
options: Military arms used by poor nations
Quiet forms of resistance like foot-dragging and sabotage

details.summary: James Scott's concept of everyday resistance describes how subordinate groups resist domination through foot-dragging, feigned ignorance, sabotage, gossip, and hidden transcripts. These quiet acts of defiance are far more common than open rebellion and can be equally politically significant.
details.whyItMatters: Everyday resistance reveals that subordinate groups are never fully passive. When open rebellion is too dangerous, people resist through subtle noncompliance that cumulatively undermines domination without provoking violent repression.
takeaways: James Scott identified everyday resistance as a major political force
Subordinate groups resist through subtle acts like foot-dragging
These quiet acts cumulatively undermine dominant power structures

faq.question: What are Scott's hidden transcripts?
faq.answer: The public transcript is what subordinate groups say and do in the presence of the powerful — deference, compliance, flattery. The hidden transcript is what they say privately — criticism, mockery, anger. The gap between public and hidden transcripts reveals the reality of power relations.

faq.question: Is everyday resistance politically effective?
faq.answer: Individually, acts like working slowly or feigning misunderstanding seem trivial. Collectively, they can reduce state revenue, undermine labor productivity, and erode authority. Scott argues these everyday acts of resistance have historically been more significant than rare dramatic rebellions.
